rationale: Both reach correct stable states. A's propagation is the more principled design. It first collects every transitively dependent compute cell, then recomputes each one exactly once, only after all of its inputs have settled. That is a glitch-free, topological-order update, so callbacks fire right after each cell's single, final recomputation. A also exposes ComputeCell.value as a read-only property, so callers cannot overwrite a computed value. B uses a LIFO worklist that can evaluate cells against stale inputs and recompute them several times. It then has to snapshot original values and compare them at the end to decide which callbacks to fire, which is harder to reason about. B's ComputeCell.value is also a plain writable attribute. A's repeated scan over the dirty set is not the most efficient, and B is a little more concise, but A's approach is clearer to verify and more robust.
